title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
key_facts: Firms that help failing startups close, such as SimpleClosure and Sunset, now broker sales of the startups' code and workplace data (emails, chats, documents from Google, Notion, Figma and Slack) to AI labs, simulated-workspace vendors and tech companies building their own models.

SimpleClosure added data sales in April; its Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026; 47% of its deals now include code or data sales.
One founder, Keelan Miskell, netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and expects around $15,000 for workspace data.

In August, as part of Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor for the airline's data, including 100 million emails and 176,000 employee records, for $10 million; the airline's flight attendants' union objected on privacy grounds.
No company has yet released tests comparing real-world data with alternatives, so the performance gain is unclear and prices vary widely.

Suppliers and buyers say they scrub personal data, but attorney Greg Ewing, who advises AI startups, calls such data 'legally radioactive'; Emory law professor Ifeoma Ajunwa says there is no federal law banning such sales.
Proceeds typically go to senior creditors and investors, not employees; founders have little visibility into who buys the data and for what.
quote_evidence: Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.
No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives.
Legally, this all could get iffy.
why_it_matters_hint: Staff messages and records of closed companies are becoming AI training material, with unsettled privacy law and unproven benefit.
event_date: 13 Oct 2026 (report); the market began in April 2026
